data.description:
Found by #199's author while working around a test that would not go green. **I verified the
production half on current `main` before minting: the degraded code is still shipped.**

## What happened

MRQ-93's contract test asserts on the **literal source spelling** `requestJson('/api/v1/me/profile'`.
To satisfy that regex, production code was changed to cast the response as
`{ person: PortalPerson }` instead of using the typed generic.

**The test made the shipped code less type-safe, and the test was green throughout.**

Current `main`, `src/ui/portal/PortalPage.tsx:593`:

```ts
await requestJson("/api/v1/me/profile", { method: "PATCH", body: JSON.stringify(body) });
```

No generic. That is the shape the regex demanded, and it is what is running.

#199 fixes it in the right direction: the regex now accepts the optional generic while still
checking the shared write path exists, and production restores
`requestJson<{ person: PortalPerson }>(...)`.

From #199's author, verbatim: *"That was a type-safety regression caused by the test, not an API
requirement."*

## Why this is a ticket and not a note

There is already a known follow-up that MRQ-169's contract test asserts source text across five
page files and would fail on a rename. **This changes the argument for it.** That style of test is
not merely brittle:

> **It has already degraded production code once, silently, in the direction of less safety.**

A test that can only stay green if the code gets worse is a defect in the test. It applies pressure
in a direction nobody chose, it does so invisibly, and it will do it again — a green suite is
exactly what it produces while doing it.

Note the shape: this is the night's recurring failure inverted. Everywhere else we found guarantees
with no live path — a declaration with no call site, a check that cannot fail. **This is a check
that fires perfectly and enforces the wrong thing.**

## Scope

**Enumerate the source-text-asserting contract tests, and for each ask whether the shipped code has
been shaped to satisfy the string rather than the behaviour.**

Sizing, measured rather than guessed — 20 test files read source files as text
(`read("src/…` / `readFile(… "src/…`), with a control: the same pattern over `migrations/` returns
0, so the search is discriminating rather than matching everything. `tests/node/onboarding-column-widths.test.mjs`
is in that set and is the file whose CNT-07 assertion I already flagged this week for proving a
call site exists rather than that the helper sorts.

For each of the 20, the question is not "is this test brittle" but **"has production been bent to
satisfy it"** — a rename is an inconvenience, a type cast is a regression. Report the files you
checked and **cleared**, not only the ones you changed; a list of "these are fine" is the evidence
the sweep happened.

Two known: MRQ-169's five-file test (rename-fragile, not yet shown to have bent anything) and
MRQ-93's (bent production, confirmed). **MRQ-93's was found by accident**, when someone had to work
around it. The others are found by grepping, not by waiting for the next accident.

## What to do with each finding

Not "delete the test". Source-text assertions have a legitimate job here — several of them pin CSS
rules and rendered class names that no type system or unit test can see, which is precisely the
class of defect the merge guard exists for. The fix is to **assert the property, not the spelling**:
accept the forms that satisfy the contract, and where a behavioural test can carry the same
guarantee, move it there and say so.

## Acceptance

- The 20 source-text-asserting test files are enumerated, each marked bent / brittle / fine, with
  the reasoning.
- Every case where production was shaped to satisfy a string is restored to the better form and its
  assertion widened to accept it.
- A regression test for at least the MRQ-93 case that fails if the generic is stripped again.
- No test is deleted without saying what guarantee it was carrying and where that guarantee now
  lives.

## Constraints

- Cut your worktree from `github/main`; CLAUDE.md now carries the correct instruction. Verify:
  `if git fetch github; then if git merge-base --is-ancestor github/main HEAD; then echo current; else echo 'behind -- rebase'; fi; else echo 'FETCH FAILED -- not attempted'; fi`
- **Never `git stash` anywhere in this repo** — the stash stack is shared across every worktree.
- **Push when the work is written, before the verification run.**
- **A red gate is real.** `fail` from a findings-derived check is load-invariant; `pass-over-budget`
  is a warn; `timeout` is the only status contention can manufacture. Never dismiss failing tests as
  a baseline without naming the commit that made them pass.
- Gate through `/Users/atin/Projects/Stage11/deployments/Marquee-worktrees/.gate-lock/gate-lock.sh`.
- Test titles start with `CONTRACT` or `AC-<n>`, then a middle dot.
- No migration. Do not deploy.

data.body:
LIVE BLOCKING INSTANCE, and it changes this ticket's urgency from 'has degraded code once' to 'is blocking work right now'.

#205 (MRQ-180, CNT-08) is RED on exactly this class:

  tests/node/bulk-paths.AC-66-69.test.mjs:361
  expected: /recipientsFor/
  actual:   the full source text of sendComms
  ERR_ASSERTION, status 'fail'

The test reads sendComms as text and asserts the literal string 'recipientsFor' appears in it. The MRQ-180 refactor replaced that call with resolveReminderSelection. The behaviour is correct and better; the spelling changed. A source-text contract test is blocking a correct refactor because it pinned a name.

That makes three instances with three distinct failure modes, which is the argument for sweeping all 31 rather than fixing the ones we tripped over:

  MRQ-93   — the test BENT PRODUCTION: forced a cast instead of a typed generic, and shipped it.
             Still on main at PortalPage.tsx:593; the restoration is unmerged on #199.
  MRQ-178  — the test PROVED NOTHING: onboarding-column-widths.test.mjs asserted the call site
             exists, and would have passed with the comparator inverted.
  MRQ-180  — the test BLOCKED A CORRECT CHANGE: pinned a function name across a refactor.

Degrade, no-op, obstruct. One technique, three ways of being wrong, and only the second is the one people expect when they hear 'brittle test'.

I have told #205's implementer NOT to simply update the string to resolveReminderSelection — that is the cheap fix that looks correct and re-arms the trap for the next rename. Assert the property, or widen the pattern and say why the name is load-bearing.

To satisfy that regex, production code was changed to cast the response as
`{ person: PortalPerson }` instead of using the typed generic.

**The test made the shipped code less type-safe, and the test was green throughout.**

Current `main`, `src/ui/portal/PortalPage.tsx:593`:

```ts
await requestJson("/api/v1/me/profile", { method: "PATCH", body: JSON.stringify(body) });
```

No generic. That is the shape the regex demanded, and it is what is running.

#199 fixes it in the right direction: the regex now accepts the optional generic while still
checking the shared write path exists, and production restores
`requestJson<{ person: PortalPerson }>(...)`.

From #199's author, verbatim: *"That was a type-safety regression caused by the test, not an API
requirement."*

## Why this is a ticket and not a note

There is already a known follow-up that MRQ-169's contract test asserts source text across five
page files and would fail on a rename. **This changes the argument for it.** That style of test is
not merely brittle:

> **It has already degraded production code once, silently, in the direction of less safety.**

A test that can only stay green if the code gets worse is a defect in the test. It applies pressure
in a direction nobody chose, it does so invisibly, and it will do it again — a green suite is
exactly what it produces while doing it.

Note the shape: this is the night's recurring failure inverted. Everywhere else we found guarantees
with no live path — a declaration with no call site, a check that cannot fail. **This is a check
that fires perfectly and enforces the wrong thing.**

## Scope

**Enumerate the source-text-asserting contract tests, and for each ask whether the shipped code has
been shaped to satisfy the string rather than the behaviour.**

**Sweep size: 31 test files.** Re-run it rather than trusting this number — the pattern is here
precisely so you do not have to:

```sh
git grep -lE 'read(File|FileSync)?\(.*"src/' -- tests        # 31
git grep -lE 'read(File|FileSync)?\(.*"migrations/' -- tests #  3, a strict SUBSET of the 31
```

The 3 that read `migrations/` — `audit-request-id.test.mjs`, `form-field-dates.test.mjs`,
`reviewer-boundary.AC-214-246.test.mjs` — all also read `src/`, confirmed with `comm`. They are
worth naming as a labelled subset rather than an addition, because reading a schema as text is the
same technique aimed at a different target, and **"a schema shaped to satisfy a string"** is a
failure worth being able to say out loud.

`tests/node/onboarding-column-widths.test.mjs` is in the 31, and is the file whose CNT-07 assertion
was already flagged for proving a call site exists rather than that the helper sorts.

**The control, and why the first two were worthless.** Run over `scripts/`:

```sh
git grep -lE 'read(File|FileSync)\(' -- scripts          # 13 files read something
git grep -lE 'read(File|FileSync)?\(.*"src/' -- scripts  #  1 reads src/ as text
```

That control *can* fire and does — once — which is stronger evidence than a clean zero, because it
proves the pattern finds the thing when the thing is present.

The two controls it replaces both failed, in instructive ways. The first ran the pattern over
`migrations/` and got 0 — but `migrations/` holds **20 files, none of them non-`.sql`**, so a
JavaScript call-expression pattern could never have matched there. **A control incapable of
returning anything but zero, reported as evidence of discrimination.** The second used the literal
`read(`, which does not match `readFile(` or `readFileSync(` at all, and so returned 0 for the
wrong reason.

**Four people measured this number and the first three were wrong** — 20, then 23, then 20 again,
now 31. One pattern missed `readFileSync`, one used too narrow a literal, and one reconciliation
missed that the two sets overlap. That is why the commands are written above the number: **the
figure nobody could pin down is exactly the figure everyone was about to quote.**

For each of the 31, the question is not "is this test brittle" but **"has production been bent to
satisfy it"** — a rename is an inconvenience, a type cast is a regression. Report the files you
checked and **cleared**, not only the ones you changed; a list of "these are fine" is the evidence
the sweep happened.

Two known: MRQ-169's five-file test (rename-fragile, not yet shown to have bent anything) and
MRQ-93's (bent production, confirmed). **MRQ-93's was found by accident**, when someone had to work
around it. The others are found by grepping, not by waiting for the next accident.

## What to do with each finding

Not "delete the test". Source-text assertions have a legitimate job here — several of them pin CSS
rules and rendered class names that no type system or unit test can see, which is precisely the
class of defect the merge guard exists for. The fix is to **assert the property, not the spelling**:
accept the forms that satisfy the contract, and where a behavioural test can carry the same
guarantee, move it there and say so.

## Acceptance

- The 31 source-text-asserting test files are enumerated, each marked bent / brittle / fine, with
  the reasoning.
- Every case where production was shaped to satisfy a string is restored to the better form and its
  assertion widened to accept it.
- A regression test for at least the MRQ-93 case that fails if the generic is stripped again.
- No test is deleted without saying what guarantee it was carrying and where that guarantee now
  lives.

## Constraints

- Cut your worktree from `github/main`; CLAUDE.md now carries the correct instruction. Verify:
  `if git fetch github; then if git merge-base --is-ancestor github/main HEAD; then echo current; else echo 'behind -- rebase'; fi; else echo 'FETCH FAILED -- not attempted'; fi`
- **Never `git stash` anywhere in this repo** — the stash stack is shared across every worktree.
- **Push when the work is written, before the verification run.**
- **A red gate is real.** `fail` from a findings-derived check is load-invariant; `pass-over-budget`
  is a warn; `timeout` is the only status contention can manufacture. Never dismiss failing tests as
  a baseline without naming the commit that made them pass.
- Gate through `/Users/atin/Projects/Stage11/deployments/Marquee-worktrees/.gate-lock/gate-lock.sh`.
- Test titles start with `CONTRACT` or `AC-<n>`, then a middle dot.
- No migration. Do not deploy.

**One technique, three distinct ways of being wrong — and only the third is what anyone pictures
when they hear "brittle test."**

| instance | how the test failed |
|---|---|
| **MRQ-93** | **BENT PRODUCTION** — forced a cast instead of a typed generic, and shipped it. Still on `main` at `PortalPage.tsx:593`; the restoration is unmerged on #199. |
| **MRQ-178** | **PROVED NOTHING** — `onboarding-column-widths.test.mjs` asserted a call site exists; it passes with the comparator inverted. |
| **MRQ-180** | **BLOCKED A FIX** — pinned a function name across a correct refactor. Red on #205 right now. |

**Degrade, no-op, obstruct.** That is the argument for sweeping all 31 rather than fixing the ones
we trip over: **two of the three modes are invisible until you go looking**, because a no-op test
is green and a bent production line compiles. Only the obstructing one announces itself, and it
announces itself as *your* problem rather than the test's.

data.body:
MODEL ANSWER NOW DEMONSTRATED, NOT RECOMMENDED — and add one file to the set.

#205's AST-walk replacement was MUTATION-TESTED by its reviewer before merge: it survives a rename of the function, and it FAILS when the await is dropped. Both directions. That was the check that mattered, because a structural test which only survives renames and never fails on broken structure is failure mode two from this ticket's own table wearing better clothes. It does both, so the pattern in the earlier worked-example comment is now evidence rather than advice. Merged as c8328a80cce4.

That is the standard for the remaining files: after you rewrite an assertion, rename the thing it names and confirm it still passes, then break the structure it claims to pin and confirm it fails. A rewrite that only does the first has moved the defect, not fixed it.

ALSO: tests/node/onboarding-column-widths.test.mjs was flagged again by #205's reviewer as a source-text reader. It IS already inside the 31 — I confirmed it in the set when I sized the sweep — but it is worth naming explicitly in the ticket because it has now been independently identified twice by different agents, which makes it the most likely place to find a fourth instance.

ADD tests/node/r2-cors.MRQ-92.test.mjs (or whichever file carries the new r2-cors assertions from #221) to the sweep set if it is not already in the 31.

Flagged by #221's reviewer: the new r2-cors.MRQ-92 assertions are source-text regex — this ticket's pattern. It did the right thing and independently verified the real render matches, so the coverage is SOUND TODAY even though the mechanism is the brittle one.

That distinction is worth keeping when the sweep runs: a source-text assertion that currently agrees with reality is not yet any of the three failure modes. It is a candidate for all of them — it will not notice a rename, it proves nothing about behaviour, and it can be satisfied by shaping the code. Classify it as at-risk rather than defective, and say which of the 31 fall in that category versus which have already bent, no-oped or blocked something. A sweep that reports 31 defects when it found 3 defects and 28 hazards will get the wrong response from whoever reads it.

MERGE CAPTAIN — a fourth way a coverage check reads clean while being wrong (2026-08-14, found by Defect Sweep 2 during the eval-11 merge run)

This ticket catalogues tests that do not test what they claim. Here is the same failure one layer up, in the tool meant to CATCH that. Filed as a comment rather than a new ticket, under the operator's pause on new tickets.

THE HOLE: 'npm run trace:ac -- --scope=merged' catches an AC with NO tests. It does NOT catch a test on the WRONG AC.

OBSERVED, not hypothesised. New tests on fix/spk07-portal-open were titled 'AC-284 · …'. AC-284 is REAL — it belongs to instance-status configuration reporting. So ac-coverage.json silently REASSIGNED that AC to the new file and listed four unrelated tests as its coverage. trace:ac reported no error and no warning: the id exists, so the tracer simply attributes it.

WHY IT IS WORSE THAN A MISSING TEST. It reads as clean AND it destroys evidence. AC-284 appeared covered by tests that have nothing to do with it, while the tests that genuinely cover it — tests/integration/cold-start.AC-275-286.test.ts and tests/node/cold-start-docs.AC-281-284-287.test.mjs — were displaced from its coverage. Nobody discovers this until the AC fails in production and the trace insists it was covered. A missing test is visible; a stolen attribution is not.

PROPOSED DETECTION (Defect Sweep 2's, written down rather than built): the mistake has a mechanical shape — an AC gains its coverage from a test file sharing no lineage with that AC's ticket. The genuine AC-284 files carry the AC number in their FILENAMES; the impostor was portal-preview-exchange.eval11.test.ts, which carries no AC lineage at all. So: if an AC's covering tests come only from files whose names reference no AC and no shared ticket, emit a WARNING. Warn, not fail — legitimate cases exist — but it would have surfaced this one immediately.

INTERIM RULE, in force across the fleet from tonight: title tests 'CONTRACT · <TICKET> · …' unless you are DELIBERATELY claiming a specific AC you own and have verified belongs to your ticket. An invented-but-colliding id is invisible to the check.

Related from the same run: 'MRQ-XXX · ' is not an accepted trace:ac prefix at all and cost five PRs a full CI round trip each — that failure is at least loud. This one is silent, which is why it belongs in this ticket's family.

THREE VERIFICATION COMMANDS THAT LOOK LIKE COVERAGE AND ARE NOT (merge run, 2026-08-14)

This ticket is about techniques that resemble verification without being it. Tonight produced three at the COMMAND level rather than the test level — each one a check an agent ran, read as green, and was wrong about. All three are observed, each cost at least one CI round trip, and one of them survived a full adversarial review.

1. A BARE 'npx tsc --noEmit' NEVER SEES THE CLIENT GRAPH.
   It reads tsconfig.json alone. tsconfig.client.json declares types: ["vite/client"], so a src/lib module imported by the browser compiles under one config and not the other.
   OBSERVED on PR #268: src/lib/demo-mail-allowlist.ts is imported by the UI panel and leaned on D1Database as an AMBIENT GLOBAL, which exists only under tsconfig.json. It would not compile for the client.
   WHY IT IS THE WORST OF THE THREE: it survived two earlier green runs AND a full adversarial review round. The reviewer ran 'vite build' and grepped dist/ to clear the bundle question — and could not have caught it, BECAUSE THE BUNDLE WAS FINE. Only the typecheck was not. A passing build is not a passing client typecheck.
   EXPOSURE: any PR touching a src/lib module the UI imports. The fix is the existing convention — import the type by name; nine shared modules already do (venues, public-schedules, person-profile, …).

2. 'npx vitest' DOES NOT RUN tests/node/*.test.mjs.
   Those are node --test .mjs files and no vitest config includes them. They hold the source-text and AST contracts — WIPE_ORDER, product-table counts, session-writer counts, the SKILL.md generator contracts.
   OBSERVED on PR #266: the builder ran 'npx vitest run --config vitest.node.config.ts', read '96 files / 640 tests' as covering tests/node, and went red on CI on two contracts that command never executed. The config name makes this actively misleading.
   Run 'node --test tests/node/*.test.mjs' explicitly. ~40s, lock-free.

3. 'trace:ac' CATCHES AN AC WITH NO TESTS, NOT A TEST ON THE WRONG AC.
   Already filed above in detail. Restated here because it belongs with the other two: a real-but-unrelated AC id is attributed silently, with no error and no warning, and displaces the genuine coverage.

THE SHAPE THEY SHARE, which is this ticket's subject one level up: each command answers a NARROWER question than the one the agent believed it was asking. 'tsc passes' means one project. 'vitest passes' means one runner. 'trace:ac passes' means every id exists. None of them is the sentence the agent wrote in its PR body.

STANDING PRE-PUSH BAR adopted across the fleet tonight, which closes 1 and 2 and mitigates 3:
  npx tsc -p tsconfig.json --noEmit
  npx tsc -p tsconfig.client.json --noEmit
  npx tsc -p tsconfig.test.json --noEmit
  npm run check:schema            (if migrations or FKs are touched)
  npm run trace:ac -- --scope=merged
  node --test tests/node/*.test.mjs
  targeted vitest on touched files
All lock-free, no gate lock, seconds to ~40s. Between them these caught: a test-types error that failed CI in 30 seconds, a client-graph error invisible to build and review, two stale generated-file contracts, and five PRs' worth of title-prefix failures.

PR #271 merged as 0963729e957a315733faa02bcbde9f6b81362659 from exact head 740843c7e9307e690f2478f2e8e8cc0c1d9a5404. Hosted fast-gate passed: new source-text test guard, three typechecks, build, design, clocks, schema, full npm test, and merged AC trace. Local proof: 59 known offender files remain with 0 new; temporary unlisted offender failed with 1 new; copy-only real control stayed clean; node tests passed 246/246. No deployment performed.
